PSA levels can be an indicator for higher risk of prostate cancer or existing prostate cancer).
A number of trials have attempted to investigate the effect of b-carotene supplementation on nonmelanoma skin cancer, the
most common forms of which are basal cell and squamous cell carcinomas (these types of cells are both found in the top layer
of the skin). However, none have shown any signiﬁcant effect on skin cancer prevention. For example, the PHS found no effect after
12 years of b-carotene supplementation on the development of a ﬁrst nonmelanoma skin cancer. The Nambour Skin Cancer Preven-
tion Trial (NSCPT) of 1621 men and women followed for nearly 5 years (most of whom had no history of skin cancer at baseline)
showed that those supplemented with 30 mg b-carotene did not experience any reduction in risk of basal cell or squamous cell
carcinoma or the occurrence of solar keratoses (precancerous skin growths that are a strong determinant of squamous cell carci-
noma). The SUVIMAX found no effect of low-dose b-carotene along with vitamin C, vitamin E, selenium, and zinc on risk of
